title: Project: budget & expense tracker
goal: Build a monthly tracker: set up categories, total spending by category and month with SUMIFS, show each category as a share of income, warn when a budget is nearly used, and work out how long a savings goal will take.

steps.text:
Kavya earns ₹40,000 a month in Bengaluru and wants to know where it goes. This is the tracker you'll build: every category has a **budget**, what she **spent**, what's **left**, its share of her income and a warning when she's close to the limit.

You'll set up the categories, total her expense log with a formula, add the percentages and warnings, then check a savings goal. Work on your own: clues are there if you get stuck.

steps.prompt:
Start with the list everything else will depend on. Type Kavya's four categories and monthly budgets in `A2:B5`, one row at a time ([[Tab]] between the cells, [[Enter]] at the end of a row):

• Food 5500
• Rent 12000
• Travel 2000
• Fun 2000
steps.explain: These four names are now the **single list** of categories. Later you'll point a drop-down at `A2:A5` (Data → Data Validation → List), so only these exact names can ever be typed into her log.

wrongFeedback.textNotNumber: A budget must be a plain number: only digits, no ₹ and no commas.
wrongFeedback.empty: Something is still blank. Each category needs a name in column A and a number in column B.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Check each row against the list: the name in column A, the number in column B.

clues: Click `A2`, type Food, Tab, 5500, Enter. Then repeat for the next row.

steps.prompt: Kavya's expense log for March and April is in `E:G`. In ==C2==, work out how much she spent on **Food in March**. Point at the category in `A2`, and lock the log ranges with `$` (press [[F4]] while the range is selected, or just type the dollar signs) so the formula can be copied down later.
steps.explain: **6000**: the two March Food rows, 3200 + 2800. April's 3600 stays out because of the month condition, and all of March's other categories stay out because of the category condition.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Formulas start with `=`. Type it again, beginning with `=`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket, comma and quote mark.
wrongFeedback.missingFunction: You need to add amounts that match **two** things (category and month). That's SUMIFS: the numbers to add first, then each range with its condition.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Food in **March** only. April's Food (3600) shouldn't be in, and nor should other categories. Is each condition in your formula?

clues: Add the Paid column. Condition 1: Category equals `A2`. Condition 2: Month equals "Mar".

steps.prompt:
Your formula is in `C2` and `C2:C5` is selected. Copy it down to Rent, Travel and Fun.

Thanks to the `$` signs, the log ranges stay put while `A2` slides down to `A3`, `A4` and `A5`.

One row in the log says **Foood** (three o's), so Food shows 3200 instead of 6000, and nothing warns Kavya.

What's the best way to stop typos like this at the source?
options: Add a drop-down to the Category column
steps.explain: A drop-down (Data → Data Validation → Allow: List, Source `=$A$2:$A$5`) only accepts the four names from your list, so “Foood” can't be typed. SUMIFS never complains about a misspelt category: it just quietly adds nothing.
wrongFeedback: There's no error to hide: SUMIFS happily returns 3200. IFERROR can't see a typo.
Sorting would put `Foood` next to `Food`, but to SUMIFS it is still a different word.
clues: Think about preventing the typo, not hiding its effect.

steps.prompt: The log is totalled (we pasted the answers into `C2:C5`). In ==D2==, show how much of Food's budget is **left**. A negative number means she has overspent.
steps.explain: **-500**: Food's budget was 5500 and she spent 6000. The minus sign is the warning, and the other rows follow the same pattern.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Formulas start with `=`. Type it again, beginning with `=`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket, comma and quote mark.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Budget minus spent, so overspending comes out negative: `B2` take away `C2`.

clues: Budget first, then subtract what she spent.

steps.prompt: Now each category's share of Kavya's income. Her income is in `B7`. In ==E2==, divide Food's spending by her income, and lock the income cell with `$` so the formula can be copied down.
steps.explain: **0.15**, which is 15% of her ₹40,000. `$B$7` stays locked when you copy down, so every category divides by the same income. Without the `$`, row 3 would divide by `B8`, an empty cell, and show an error.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Formulas start with `=`. Type it again, beginning with `=`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket, comma and quote mark.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Divide what she spent on Food (`C2`) by her income (`B7`).

steps.prompt:
`E2:E5` are filled in but read `0.15`, `0.3`, `0.04`, `0.05`, which is hard for anyone to read. They're selected.

Make them look like percentages.
clues: The % sign lives on the 5 key.

steps.prompt: Kavya wants early warnings. The first three rows are done. In ==F5==, show **Over budget** if Fun's spending is above its budget, **Near limit** if she has used **90% or more** of it, and **OK** otherwise.
steps.explain: **Near limit**: Fun used 2000 of 2000. That isn't “over” (2000 is not more than 2000), but it's past 90%. The tests run worst first, so a category gets the first message that fits.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Formulas start with `=`. Type it again, beginning with `=`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket, comma and quote mark.
wrongFeedback.missingReference: Compare Fun's spending (`C5`) with its budget (`B5`).
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Fun spent exactly its budget. Is that over? Is it at least 90% used? Check your order of tests.

clues: Two IFs: one inside the other's “otherwise” part.

steps.prompt:
Kavya adds a conditional-formatting rule (Home → Conditional Formatting → New Rule → Use a formula) to `A2:F5`:

`=$C2>$B2`

It colours a row when **Spent is more than Budget**. Select the row that turns red.
steps.wrongFeedback: Compare Spent (column C) with Budget (column B) row by row. Only one row has Spent **above** Budget; rows where they're equal don't count.
clues: Rent and Fun spent exactly their budget. Is that “more than”?

steps.prompt:
You're typing the rule for the first row, row 2, of `A2:F5`, so that every row is judged by its **own** numbers and the whole row changes colour.

Which rule is right?
steps.explain: The `$` before each column letter locks the **column** (every cell in the row looks at C and B), while the row number stays free to move down. Mixed references like `$C2` are made for rules that colour whole rows.
wrongFeedback: Without `$`, the columns slide too: cell B2 would compare D2 with C2, and so on, so the colours would be nonsense.
`$C$2` is locked to row 2 forever, so every row would copy Food's answer.
clues: The row number should change as you go down; the column letter shouldn't.

steps.prompt: How much did Kavya **save** this month? In ==B8==, show what's left of her income after her total spending (the total is in `C6`).
steps.explain: **18400**: 40000 income minus 21600 spent. Because it points at the total in `C6`, it updates whenever an expense changes.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Formulas start with `=`. Type it again, beginning with `=`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket, comma and quote mark.

steps.prompt:
Kavya gets a raise: income becomes **48000**, and her spending stays exactly the same.

What will Rent's **% of income** (`E3`, currently 30%) become?
steps.explain: Rent is still 12000, but it's now divided by 48000, and 12000 ÷ 48000 = 0.25. Next, see whether the sheet agrees.
wrongFeedback: The percentage is a formula that divides by income, so it moves when income moves.
A bigger income makes every share **smaller**, never bigger.

steps.prompt: Now check your prediction. Click ==B7==, type **48000**, press [[Enter]], and watch `E3` and `B8`.
steps.explain: You changed one number and the whole tracker followed: Rent fell to **0.25** (25%) and savings jumped to **26400**. That's why you used formulas and `$`, instead of typing the answers.

wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Only `B7` should change, to 48000. The others will follow by themselves.

steps.prompt: Kavya's raise has come through. She wants **90000** for a laptop. If she keeps saving the same amount every month, how many whole months until she has enough? Answer in ==B6==.
steps.explain: **4 months**: 90000 ÷ 26400 is about 3.4, but after 3 months she'd have only 79200. Whole months only, so round **up**. `ROUND` or `INT` would say 3 and leave her short.

wrongFeedback.notFormula: Formulas start with `=`. Type it again, beginning with `=`.
wrongFeedback.parseError: Excel can't read that. Check every bracket, comma and quote mark.
wrongFeedback.wrongValue: Divide the goal by the monthly saving, then ask: does that many months actually get her there?

clues: Goal divided by monthly saving gives a decimal. What should you do with it?
